answer: Motorist deaths exceed cyclist deaths every year from 2013–2025, roughly 5 to 1 overall (1,377 motorists vs. 277 cyclists killed over the 13 years). Motorist deaths ranged from a low of 72 (2016) and 81 (2025) to a peak of 139 in 2020 and 134 in 2021, then generally declined to 81 by 2025. Cyclist deaths were far smaller and flatter, ranging from 10 (2018) and 11 (2013) to 31 in 2019 and 2023. The gap was widest in 2013 (110 vs. 11, 10:1) and narrowest in 2019 (82 vs. 31, 2.6:1); notably, cyclist deaths nearly tripled from 10 in 2018 to 31 in 2019 while motorist deaths fell, and by 2025 the ratio stood at 3.5:1 (81 vs. 23).

Every value I could read matches values.csv: bars 110…81, line endpoints 297 and 229, curve ≈123 at 60%, 74 at 100%, ≈61 at 120%, break-even 81/110 = 73.6% ≈ 74%, drop −26.4% ≈ −26%.
answer: Motorist (vehicle-occupant) deaths fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025, a 26% drop. Because the data has no miles-driven column, the per-mile question is answered by break-even: the risk of a motorist being killed per mile driven fell if 2025 mileage was at least ~74% of 2013's — in that case risk per mile is about 26% lower than in 2013 (it would rise only if 2025 driving fell below ~74% of 2013 levels). Caveats: the 2020–21 spike in deaths per crash, and the post-2019 halving of minor-crash reports (injuries fell only ~19–20% from 2018–19, far less than the 60% drop in reported crashes), so trends in reports alone overstate the change in exposure.
